description: We are team from Institut Teknologi Bandung that is passionate in Hackathon
summary:
Satellites now flag fire hotspots within hours, and Indonesia's fire agencies rely on them. In Central Kalimantan, where drained peat burns most dry seasons and can smoulder unseen, a district officer checks them each morning. But does zero mean no fire, or that cloud hid the ground? KalenderApi ("fire calendar" in Indonesian) answers that.

First we harmonize NASA's MODIS and VIIRS hotspots since 2000 onto one scale: a burning calendar for 34 provinces and 514 districts. Joined as recorded, fires seem to rise 95% between 2003-2007 and 2017-2021; on one scale they fall 64%. The rise was the sharper sensor.

Then we go where harmonization stops. Under cloud a satellite cannot see, so a zero can mean "not seen". From NASA's MODIS fire masks we map this by district and day over eleven fire seasons: on 1,482 of 13,510 district-days, most of the district had no cloud-free look.

"Today in my district" turns this into a command screen for the disaster office (BPBD): live NASA hotspots on a map, a level set by a published rule, and what to do now: check the newest hotspot, re-check peat sites where fire keeps coming back (18,113 on Central Kalimantan's peat), alert the village. One tap opens a ready message in Bahasa Indonesia in WhatsApp, and residents can report fire back.

We wrote our validation tests first, and we show the ones that failed.

Zero should mean "we looked", not "we could not see".
details:
The problem

Indonesia's hotspot record changes satellites in 2012, when VIIRS joins MODIS. VIIRS sees smaller fires, so a raw splice shows a surge that is mostly the sensor. A provincial disaster agency (BPBD) that asks "is this year unusual?" gets the wrong answer from the raw record. There is a second problem that harmonization does not fix. A day with zero hotspots is read as a quiet day. Under cloud, it is a day the satellite could not look.

What KalenderApi does

  • A burning calendar on one scale, November 2000 to November 2026, for Indonesia, its island regions, its provinces and 514 districts: one row per year, one column per month. Find a district by name or by latitude and longitude.
  • This month against the median of the same month, with its rank, for the area you pick.
  • A date range you choose, compared with the same months in every other year, with CSV and PNG downloads, and a CSV of the hotspots themselves for the seasons we hold.
  • The zero, day by day: for Central Kalimantan's 14 districts, a map for each day of the fire season showing where there was no cloud-free look, over that day's NASA photo and its hotspots. Twelve fire seasons are built (August to October of 2014 to 2024 and 2026; 2025 has no fire mask yet), plus one wet-season quarter for contrast.
  • A zero inspector for one district, Pulang Pisau: every 1 km cell on one day as fire, a zero with a cloud-free look, a zero without one, or no data.
  • A reporting rule the map supports: do not report "no hotspots" for a district on a day when most of it had no cloud-free look. Over eleven fire seasons that was 1,482 of 13,510 district-days (11%); in the wet-season quarter, 442 of 1,148 (39%).
  • Today in my district: for any of the 514 districts, the hotspots NASA detected in the last 24 hours and 7 days (VIIRS on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, and MODIS, from the FIRMS near-real-time files, read when the page opens), whether this month is above normal on the one-scale record, and a level (calm, watch or high) set by a rule shown on the page. It is our own rule, not an official status. The page writes three messages ready to send, for residents and the village, for the district disaster office (BPBD) and for the Manggala Agni fire crew, each with a WhatsApp button. If today's data cannot be read, no level is set: the page never calls a district calm without data.
  • Peat sites where fire comes back, for Central Kalimantan: a peat cell of about 1 km is a persistent site when VIIRS detects fire there on three or more days of a season, or again after a gap of two days or more. Over eleven fire seasons that is 18,113 persistent sites and 31,476 come-backs. For each gap we read the MODIS fire mask: in 25,259 the satellite had a cloud-free look and saw no fire, in 6,184 MODIS saw fire while VIIRS did not, 25 were under cloud throughout and 8 had no data. The Today page lists the top sites of the district with coordinates, as places to re-check on the ground. It does not say fire kept burning in the gap.
  • A printable one-page brief per area, in Bahasa Indonesia or English.
  • A story that walks through the jump, the fix and the zero in under a minute, and a day-by-day player of a whole fire season.

How the one scale is made

We count fire cell-days: one 0.01-degree cell on one day with at least one detection (vegetation fires only, low confidence removed). Counting cells instead of hotspots removes most of the difference between VIIRS's 375 m pixels and MODIS's 1 km pixels. The scale is Aqua MODIS. Through 2021 the record is Aqua's own count. From 2022, when Aqua's orbit drifts, it is VIIRS converted to the Aqua scale with factors by island region, season, day or night and peat, calibrated on 2012 to 2021, with a 90% range from 1,000 bootstrap draws. District values share their province's monthly conversion and are marked approximate.

What we found

  • Between 2003-2007 and 2017-2021, Indonesia's raw spliced record rises 95%; on one scale it falls 64%. The two readings point in opposite directions. The direction of the one-scale change does not depend on whether El Nino years are included (it is -62% without them), or on whether the comparison crosses the 2022 seam (-63%).
  • October 2026, still provisional, stands at 4.1 times the median October for Indonesia.
  • In October 2019, 17.4% of Central Kalimantan's no-fire readings had no cloud-free look, although the month as a whole counts as well observed. On the worst day we hold, 29 October 2015, the share was 79%.

What we checked, and what failed

We wrote the validation tests before the run and show every result in the app. On years held out of the calibration, the one-scale record misses by 7.2%; the raw splice misses by 435%. The 2012 switch test passes. The 2022 seam test fails, so values from 2022 are less certain than the range suggests. A simpler method does better than our chosen one on held-out years, and several regions transfer poorly. 15 tests pass, 11 fail, 9 were not run. We would rather show this than hide it.

What the zero layer is, and is not

It is the share of no-fire cell-days with no cloud-free look by MODIS (MOD14A1 and MYD14A1 fire masks). It is not a count of hidden fires. Thick smoke is not flagged as cloud, so the true unseen share is higher. It looks back in time; it is not an early warning.

Who it is for

A BPBD district officer who opens "Today in my district" in the morning, sees what the satellites detected and how far to trust a zero, and forwards a message to the village; a Manggala Agni crew that gets coordinates of the newest hotspots and of peat sites to re-check; a planner placing patrols by month; researchers who need a fire history that does not jump with the sensor. We have not yet tested it with an agency. That is the next step.

Limits

Hotspots are heat detections, not burned area. Values from 2022 rest on a seam that fails its test. District values are approximate. The zero layer and the peat sites cover one province, and the zero layer measures cloud only. The peat index is exploratory: we wrote its rule after looking at the data. The level on the Today page is our own rule. KalenderApi is not an official product and does not forecast.

Tools

Python (pandas, DuckDB) for the pipeline; TypeScript, React, Vite, deck.gl, MapLibre and Observable Plot for the app; Vercel for hosting, with two small serverless functions (one reads NASA's near-real-time hotspot files, one drafts advice with an AI model).
